value: upper bound on sensitivity of 0.0045 C/s (peak cooling rate) in L1, L2 and early L3 larvae
method: in vivo calcium imaging (GCaMP6m in the primary cold sensor neurons, strain R11F02>GCaMP6m) during sine-wave temperature modulation, amplitude 0.05 to 1.0 C, period 60 s, offset 17 C; responses compared with the zero level expected from a non-responsive neuron
conditions: larvae of three developmental stages (L1, L2, early L3), stage responses indistinguishable at the lowest amplitude and all above zero; the lowest amplitude was the smallest sine wave the equipment could generate, so 0.0045 C/s is an upper bound on the threshold, not a measured threshold; about 10 animals for each of 15 conditions (Figure 6 caption); the paper prints 'Drosophila larva' in title and methods and names D. melanogaster only in the introduction as the fruit fly model, so the record is at genus rank and graded g

source.authors: Anastasiia Evans, Anggie J. Ferrer, Erica Fradkov, Joseph W. Shomar, Josh Forer, Mason Klein
source.title: Temperature sensitivity and temperature response across development in the Drosophila larva

where: Results 3.5 (sensitivity at the sensory and behavioural levels); Methods (imaging)
quote: Thus, these measurements place an upper bound in sensitivity of 0.0045°C/s for L1, L2, and early L3 larva stages.
note: Calcium imaging, in vivo, larvae immobilised for imaging. Quote taken from a PDF read through WebFetch pieces and confirmed on a second fetch; the preceding sentence (not quoted) says the three stages' responses are indistinguishable and significantly above the zero level. Preceding Methods text gives the stimulus parameters.

value: L2 larvae turning rate at constant temperature (bin centred at 0 C/s) differed significantly from the rate at a cooling rate of -0.002 C/s
method: larvae tracked in an isotropic or linear thermal gradient arena on agar; trajectories split into bins of temperature change per time (dT/dt) and turning rates computed per bin; bin turning rates compared
conditions: L2 stage example shown as a bar graph (Figure 7C); gradient arena set linearly between 13 and 21 C on the agar gel, starting at 17 C; about 20 larvae placed near the centre per run; the +0.006 C/s warming bin also differed from adjacent bins; the paper's own conclusion is that L2 larvae are sensitive to cooling rates of at least that amount; genus-rank record as above

source.authors: Anastasiia Evans, Anggie J. Ferrer, Erica Fradkov, Joseph W. Shomar, Josh Forer, Mason Klein

source.title: Removal or component reversal of local geomagnetic field affects foraging orientation preference in migratory insect brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens

value: highest foraging orientation preference to the north direction (with the food in the north) in the geomagnetic field
method: cross-tube choice assay: adults released at the centre of a four-arm cross tube inside a coil system, arm choice recorded for 0.5 h; chi-square tests of arm distribution; geomagnetic field (GMF) compared with a near-zero field (NZMF) and a vertical-reversed field
conditions: local GMF total intensity 52,487 +/- 841 nT, inclination 56.29 deg; food placed in the north arm in this test ('original food'); 12 replicates per magnetic field setup, total insects tested 511 +/- 69, N = 241, 87, 157, 132 insects across the four arms in the GMF; lamp 15 W (320-680 nm) as light source, coils covered by a shade cloth; the next sentence of the paper gives south 14%, west 25.40% and east 21.39% (all significantly lower, p < 0.001); the preference is for the direction of the food, so it is a foraging orientation preference under a field and not a demonstrated compass heading
where: Results, Geomagnetic field (GMF), with north as the initial food direction
quote: In the GMF, N. lugens showed the highest preference of foraging orienting to the north direction with original food (χ2 = 108.48, p < 0.001).
note: Lab assay, adults within 48 h of emergence. Paper also reports that the preference disappears in the near-zero field and vertical-reversal field (separate record) and that IscA1 knockdown reduced it.

source.title: Removal or component reversal of local geomagnetic field affects foraging orientation preference in migratory insect brown planthopper Nilaparvata lugens

value: no orientation preference in a near-zero magnetic field: north 25.46%, south 22.22%, west 27.55%, east 24.77% (chi-square p = 0.088)
method: cross-tube choice assay in a coil system producing a near-zero magnetic field (NZMF); arm distribution tested by chi-square
conditions: NZMF average intensity about 500 nT at the centre of a spherical space, against a GMF of 52,487 nT; N = 110, 96, 119, 107 insects across the four arms; 12 replicates per setup; same light and shade-cloth conditions as the GMF test; the paper reports the same loss of preference under vertical component reversal of the GMF (north 25.18%, south 21.74%, west 29.53%, east 23.55%, p = 0.102)
quote: In the NZMF, however, N. lugens were relatively equally distributed and the percentage of individuals orienting to the north, south, west and east direction was 25.46%, 22.22%, 27.55% and 24.77%, respectively (χ2 = 10.261, p = 0.088) (Fig. 3B).
note: Null result in the manipulated field; read as showing that a normal field is needed for the orientation preference in the GMF record.

source.authors: Manuela Carnaghi, Steven R. Belmain, Richard J. Hopkins, Frances M. Hawkes
source.title: Multimodal synergisms in host stimuli drive landing response in malaria mosquitoes

value: with host odour and a transparent target, more mosquitoes were caught at a target set at 35 C and 45 C than at 25 C
method: wind-tunnel landing assay on a heated target, factorial treatments of visual cue (transparent or black), host odour (present or absent) and target temperature (25, 35 or 45 C); landings compared across temperatures
conditions: Anopheles coluzzii (colony from Burkina Faso, printed as An. coluzzii), non-blood-fed females four to twelve days old; arena 25 +/- 2 C and 65 +/- 5% RH; twelve treatments in all; Table 1 mean landing counts (as read through the page reader, not the table itself) were 4.8 +/- 0.88 at 25 C, 13.3 +/- 1.41 at 35 C and 11.8 +/- 1.24 at 45 C for odour with the transparent target; the paper gives no heat effect when the target is black with odour, and concludes that a thermal cue does not increase landing when odour and visual cue are both present
where: Results, Interaction between thermal cue and other host-associated cues; Table 1
quote: A higher number of mosquitoes were caught in the treatment where the transparent target was set at 35 °C and 45 °C and was presented with host odour when compared to the same target at 25 °C.
note: Behaviour, lab wind tunnel. Heat acted with odour .

source.authors: Manuela Carnaghi, Steven R. Belmain, Richard J. Hopkins, Frances M. Hawkes
source.title: Multimodal synergisms in host stimuli drive landing response in malaria mosquitoes

value: no increase in landings at 35 C or 45 C compared with 25 C for a black target with host odour
method: wind-tunnel landing assay on a heated black target with host odour present, target at 25, 35 or 45 C
conditions: same assay, species and arena as the companion record (An. coluzzii, 25 +/- 2 C arena); visual cue black and odour present, so the thermal cue added nothing in this combination; the paper concludes that a thermal cue does not increase landing if host odour and visual cue are present
where: Results, Interaction between thermal cue and other host-associated cues
quote: Furthermore, the number of landings were not different in treatments where the black surface was set at either 35 °C or 45 °C and was presented with host odour compared to the respective treatment where the temperature was 25 °C.
note: Null result from the same paper as the positive record.
